progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: b03: the chain (leave, travel, enter); direct contact, indirect contact (fomites, water, food, air) and vectors, with a vector distinguished from a fomite; "break the link". b01: pathogens multiply inside hosts. Year 11 Working Scientifically: models, variables, controls, validity, reliability, risk assessments. Not assumed: indicators, the simulation method, epidemic curves, contact tracing, the incubation period (b10 later; given here only as "a delay before someone can pass it on").
progression.startsWith: Model a safe transmission route with observable markers. The video opens: Eight students each hold a cup of clear liquid. One cup is secretly different. They share liquid with a partner, three times.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining what a model is and what each part of the fluid-exchange simulation stands for; defining an epidemic (cases above what's expected); explaining why the marker must be hidden until tested and how phenolphthalein shows the base; describing the method (equal volumes, a secret starter, new partners each round, pour all then half back, a sample saved before round one and after every round, a recorded contact sheet) and its aim and variables (contacts change; pink cups and samples are measured; volumes, pours and drops are kept the same); explaining the negative and positive controls, accuracy (the traced starter against the teacher's record) and reliability (repeat runs with a new starter); explaining why the final test cannot identify the starter; tracing the starter from saved samples and contacts, and explaining that real teams, with no start sample, use when symptoms began and contact tracing; defining an epidemic curve, plotting new cases by round, and explaining that the number infected doubled because each pink cup met a clear one (person-to-person spread), against the single peak of one shared source; describing a fluorescent powder model of indirect contact through a fomite; stating the model's limits (every contact transmits, the marker dilutes rather than multiplies, no delay before someone can pass it on, no recovery or immunity, scheduled equal contacts) and what it is valid for; writing the risk assessment; identifying possible starters from new data and assessing a claim about real spread.
progression.nextLesson: testing a water or food sample for microbes (route entry bio-m7-p02).

teaching.task: Eight students share liquid from cup to cup, three times. One cup was secretly "infected". At the end, every cup turns pink. Who started it? How do you design a safe classroom model of an epidemic that can trace the source, and what can it really tell you about how a disease spreads?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the puzzle (1); (2) what a model is, what each part stands for, and an epidemic (2); (3) why the marker must be hidden until tested, and how the indicator shows it (3); (4) the method, with the saved samples and the contact sheet (4); (5) controls and repeats (5); (6) the final test, and why it can't find the starter (6); (7) reading the well plate with the contact sheet, and contact tracing named (7); (8) the epidemic curve, doubling from person-to-person spread, against one shared source (8); (9) modelling indirect contact with fluorescent powder (9); (10) the model's limits, and what it is valid for (10); (11) risk (11); attempts (12a to 12d); decision rule and handoff (13); key notes (14).
teaching.conversationalApproach: eight students share liquid from cup to cup three times, one cup was secretly infected and at the end every cup turns pink, so the practical asks who started it, how fast it spread and what a simulation can really show. An epidemic is a rise in cases above what is expected, and the model is a simplified version of one in which each cup is a person, each mixing is a contact and the hidden marker is the pathogen. The marker must stay invisible until testing, so sodium carbonate in one cup is revealed only when phenolphthalein indicator turns it pink. The method gives each step its reason: equal volumes in numbered cups, a new partner each round, a contact sheet and a sample saved in a well plate after every round. A negative control of unmixed water and a positive control of the marker check the indicator, and repeat runs check the pattern. The final test shows who is infected now but not who was first, so the saved samples are read round by round to trace the starter, and new cases each round are plotted as an epidemic curve. Fluorescent powder on a door handle models indirect contact through a fomite. The model's limits are set against real disease (every contact transmits, nothing multiplies, no immunity or recovery), and the risk assessment follows. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Eight students each hold a cup of clear liquid. One cup is secretly different. They share liquid with a partner, three times. Then a drop of indicator goes into every cup, and all eight turn pink. So who started it? From the final colours alone, you can't tell. Let's design the model so that you can, and see what it really shows about an epidemic.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1, identify and justify, plus a method change; 4 marks) six students P to U, two rounds, final pink P, Q, R, T: the starter is P or Q (R or T would have infected S or U; S and U are clear, so they cannot be the starter); P and Q cannot be told apart because they mixed in round one; testing a sample from each cup saved before round one would identify it (a sample after round one would not: P and Q mixed in round one, so both are pink; Revision 2, LR 4). Crossed mistake: "P, because P is listed first". (A2, assess a claim; 3 marks) "The model shows that a real disease would infect everyone in a class within three rounds of contact." Answer: overreaches; in the model every contact transmits and everyone meets a new person each round, so cases double; real contacts do not always transmit, some people are immune, there is a delay before people can pass it on and people mix unevenly, so real spread depends on the disease and the group; the model does show how quickly linked contacts can multiply cases. Crossed mistake: "the model is useless because it uses chemicals, not germs" (the surface difference is not the reason; the mechanism differences are). Each improvement or judgement addresses the stated problem (owner rule).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "describe a variety of infectious diseases caused by pathogens, including microorganisms, macroorganisms and non-cellular pathogens, and collect primary and secondary-sourced data and information relating to disease transmission, including: (ACSBL097, ACSBL098, ACSBL116, ACSBL117); investigating the transmission of a disease during an epidemic; investigate modes of transmission of infectious diseases, including direct contact, indirect contact and vector transmission" this video prepares students to run the simulation, record it, analyse it and judge it; watching it is not conducting it. It teaches: what a model is and what each part of this model stands for; why the marker must be hidden until tested (an indicator); the method (equal volumes, a secret starter, rounds of mixing, a recorded contact sheet, a sample saved in a well plate before round one and after every round); the two controls and repeat runs; testing the cups, then the well plate; tracing the source from timing and contacts; the epidemic curve (new cases against time) and the doubling, person-to-person shape, against a single shared source; a variant for indirect contact (fluorescent powder on a door handle, an ultraviolet torch); the model's limits; the risk assessment. Placement (playlist order 4): after b03 (order 3), before p02 (order 5). Not re-taught: the three links and the three modes, and fomites (b03, one recall clause each). Not here: contact tracing and quarantine as control measures (b10: one recall line here, as a name for what health teams do); incidence, prevalence and outbreak tables (g01); Camp Wollemi (L04 Activity 2; its agent and timing are flagged as site errors 6 and 7 in b03, so g01 decides whether to use it); Snow (b14).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key: infected or pink amber; uninfected grey; controls green; the starter teal outline; limits terracotta; grey for tags and callbacks. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: the explainer kit (`Plate`, `Callout`, `Mark`, `Countdown`, `HandText`, `DrawPath`, `scribbleEllipse`, `Enter`); B6a's `WrongChip`, `GreyTag`, `Cross`, `Cam`; bio-m5-p01's method step rail; bio-m6-p01's VRA card and risk table layout (as reused in `bio-m7-p02.md`); b03's route board (leave, travel, enter), drawn small in scene 2. New coded items (lesson-local): the cup row (eight copies of the cup plate under coded letter chips A to H, each able to crossfade to its aligned pink copy in place), the pour arc (a coded liquid arc from one cup to another and half back, with a grey round counter), the contact sheet (a coded grid drawn over the clipboard plate: rows A to H, columns "round 1", "round 2", "round 3", filling with partner letters), the trace overlay (a coded column wipe that reveals one row of the painted well plate at a time, with coded arrows between partners), the epidemic curve (a coded bar graph that builds bar by bar), the attempt cards and answer tables. No human figures.
